summary: This document registers the application/cms media type for use with Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS wraps content in nested layers, each with its own identifier. This RFC registers a media type for such content, with two parameters: one naming the wrapping layer and one naming the innermost content. It also creates two lists of the known layer names.

questions: how to identify cms protected files
subtitle: A media type for Cryptographic Message Syntax content, and the two parameters that name its layers.

tldr.problem: The media type registered for S/MIME content carries a single smime-type parameter, which assumed that each piece of content had its own MIME wrapping layer. Some newer CMS content types break that assumption, so the type of the content inside the wrappers can no longer be told from the type outside them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the media type application/cms with two optional parameters. encapsulatingContent names the CMS content type that wraps the content, and innerContent names the type at the bottom, and each may hold a list of values.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that registers a media type with IANA and creates two registries of CMS content type names, allocated by Expert Review. The rule that separates them is simple: an inner content type does not encapsulate another content type, an encapsulating one does.

today: RFC 7193 is an Informational RFC published in April 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the registration of the application/cms media type and the definition of the two CMS content type registries.

sections.title: Why a New Media Type
sections.content:
RFC 5751 registered the media type application/pkc7-mime and defined five optional smime-type parameters. The smime-type parameter originally conveyed details about the security applied to the data content type, indicating whether it was signed or enveloped, and the name of the data content. It was later expanded to indicate whether the data content is compressed and whether it contained a certs-only message. This document does not affect those registrations, and it places no requirements on S/MIME agents.

The reason a new media type is needed is that the S/MIME registration assumed there would be a MIME wrapping layer around each of the different enveloping contents, so there was never a need to include more than one item in each smime-type. That is no longer true with some of the more advanced enveloping types. Some protocols, such as Certificate Management over Cryptographic Message Syntax, have defined additional S/MIME types. New protocols that intend to wrap MIME content should continue to define an smime-type string, while new protocols that intend to wrap non-MIME types should use the mechanism this document defines.

CMS associates a content type identifier, an object identifier, with specific content. CMS content types have been widely used to define contents that can be enveloped using other CMS content types, and to define enveloping content types, some of which provide security services. The document lists them in three groups: protecting content types, which provide security services, such as Signed-Data, Enveloped-Data, Digested-Data, Encrypted-Data, Authenticated-Data, Authenticated-Enveloped-Data and Encrypted Key Package; non-protecting content types, which provide no security services but encapsulate other CMS content types, such as Content Information, Compressed Data, Content Collection and Content With Attributes; and the innermost content types, such as Data, Asymmetric Key Package, Symmetric Key Package, the firmware package types, Trust Anchor List, the TAMP status and update types, and the key package receipt and error types.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS content sits in nested layers, and the label on the outside used to be enough to describe what was inside. Newer kinds of content have several layers at once, so the label has to name them separately.

sections.title: The Media Type and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The registration application gives the type name as application and the subtype name as cms. There are no required parameters and two optional ones, and they are case sensitive.

The encapsulatingContent parameter takes one or more CMS Encapsulating Content Type identifiers. Multiple values are enclosed in quotes and separated by a folding-whitespace, a comma and folding-whitespace. The values are based on the content types found in the CMS, compressed data, protecting multiple contents, authenticated-enveloped-data and encrypted key package documents, and the list can later be extended. The parameter innerContent works the same way for one or more CMS Inner Content Type identifiers, based on the content types found in the firmware package, trust anchor format, trust anchor management protocol, asymmetric key package, symmetric key package and key package receipt documents.

The encoding is binary, and CMS requires that the outermost encapsulation be ContentInfo. The Content-Type header field of all application/cms objects SHOULD include the optional encapsulatingContent and innerContent parameters. The Content-Disposition header field can also be included along with the Content-Type optional name parameter. The registered file extension is .cmsc, there is no magic number, the intended usage is COMMON, and there are no restrictions on usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The type is application/cms. Two optional parameters name the layers: one for the wrapping content type and one for the content at the bottom. Both can carry several values at once.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of an encrypted status response message, showing the headers that carry the media type and its two parameters, together with the base64 transfer encoding of the body.

The Content-Type header names the subtype, then the encapsulatingContent parameter with the value encryptedData, then the innerContent parameter with the value TAMP-statusResponse, and finally the optional name parameter giving the file name status.cmsc. The body itself is the CMS structure, base64 encoded for transport.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a TAMP status response wrapped in encrypted data. The header says both: which wrapper is used and what is inside it.

sections.title: The Two Registries
sections.content:
IANA has registered the media type application/cms in the Standards tree using the application in Section 2 of the document.

IANA has also established two subtype registries, called CMS Encapsulating Content Types and CMS Inner Content Types. Entries in both are allocated by Expert Review. The expert decides whether a content belongs in one or the other, and the rule is that an inner content type does not encapsulate another content type while an encapsulating content type does encapsulate another content type.

The initial values for the encapsulating registry are authData, compressedData, contentCollection, contentInfo, contentWithAttrs, authEnvelopedData, encryptedKeyPkg, digestData, encryptedData, envelopedData and signedData, each with the object identifier defined in the document that specifies it. The inner registry starts with firmwarePackage, firmwareLoadReceipt, firmwareLoadError, aKeyPackage, sKeyPackage, trustAnchorList, the twelve TAMP status and update types, and keyPackageReceipt and keyPackageError.
sections.plainLanguage: Two IANA lists hold the layer names. The rule for choosing a list is simple: if the layer wraps something else it goes in the encapsulating list, and if it does not it goes in the inner list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of the RFC points back to the answers given in the registration template of Section 2, which set out the content types and algorithms each protecting content type is defined with, and the interoperability considerations for each of them. In all cases CMS content types are encapsulated within ContentInfo structures, so the outermost enveloping structure is always ContentInfo, and the media type uses the CMS processing rules rather than the slightly different ones that PKCS #7 defines for SignedData.

Two general points are made. In some circumstances significant information can be leaked by disclosing what the innermost ASN.1 structure is, and in those cases it is acceptable to disclose the wrappers without disclosing the inner content type. And ASN.1 encoding rules, such as DER and BER, have a type-length-value structure, so it is easy to construct malicious content with invalid length fields that can cause buffer overrun conditions; the rules also allow arbitrary levels of nesting, which may make it possible to construct malicious content that causes a stack overflow. Interpreters of ASN.1 structures should guard against buffer overflows and stack overruns in particular, and against malicious content in general.
sections.plainLanguage: Naming the innermost layer can leak information, so the parameters can be left out. The bigger risk is in the ASN.1 parsing itself: bad length fields and deep nesting can overflow a buffer or a stack.

root.note: Each layer is identified by an object identifier

data.title: An encrypted status response
data.code:
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: application/cms; encapsulatingContent=encryptedData;
              innerContent=TAMP-statusResponse; name=status.cmsc
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
